summary: Offers views from MITRE and IBM authors on data sharing across the ARPANET. They support the idea of a committee to classify the issues, integrate separate data activities and coordinate experiments, as suggested by Arie Shoshani.

eli5.summary: A few people write that, yes, a group should be formed to help computers share data, and they say what it should do.

subtitle: A position paper backing a committee to bring order to data sharing on the ARPA Network.

tldr.problem: Several independent ARPA Network projects were tackling data handling, with no shared plan to make them fit together.
tldr.mechanism: The authors back a data sharing committee, describe three stages of data access, and list areas of development and experiments the committee should coordinate.
tldr.outcome: The paper is a discussion input for the data sharing meeting scheduled for Tuesday, May 18, not a protocol specification.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 146 as Unknown and it has no obsoleting or updating RFCs. It is a 1971 discussion paper rather than a specification.

sections.title: The Case for a Data Sharing Committee
sections.content:
Karp, McKay and Wood agree with the suggestion by Arie Shoshani in RFC 140 that a committee on data sharing is desirable at this point of network development. They say the committee should do three things: classify the issues and propose approaches, integrate the independent network activities that touch data sharing, and set up and coordinate experiments to test services and compare alternatives.

The paper is meant to augment Shoshani's as a basis for discussion at the data sharing meeting. It does not discuss specific implementations, only what the committee's role should be.
sections.eli5: Lots of people are building separate tools for sharing data. The writers say one group should sort out the problems and make the tools work together.

sections.title: Three Stages of Data Access
sections.content:
The authors describe three stages, which roughly match modes of use. They are not necessarily reached in order.

  • Stage 1: data services run at various Hosts, and the user reaches the serving Host directly, through TELNET or a known socket. Examples named are the file transfer system in RFC 122 and the data machine at CCA.
  • Stage 2: the user goes through an intermediate process, a data control facility, that routes requests to the serving system. The user must still name the services to use.
  • Stage 3: the user treats the network as a single resource and refers to everything by name. The data control facility acts as a referral center and combines services as needed.

The network machine notion of RFC 51 is described as closest to Stage 3.
sections.eli5: First you phone each library yourself. Then a helper phones the right library for you. At the end you just ask for a book by name and the helper finds it.

sections.title: Areas of Development
sections.content:
The paper lists areas where work is needed: a data description language to define the physical structure of files, define logical files and categorize fields for name referencing; a control or access language that can be mapped into various data management languages; and methods for managing and merging distributed data, searching file directories and recovering from errors.

Existing Stage 1 work should fit into the overall scheme. For example, the data reconfiguration service of RFC 138 would be invoked by the data control facility whenever data transformations are required, and the file transfer protocol should be consistent with other data handling services.
sections.eli5: Everyone needs a common way to describe their files, a common way to ask for things, and ways to fix mistakes. Then the separate tools can team up.

sections.title: Proposed Experiments
sections.content:
The authors want a coordinated effort to exercise each implementation alone and together with other services, and to evaluate alternative approaches. Their examples are file transfer between differently controlled systems, moving existing data bases onto the data computer, defining logical restructuring of data while keeping the physical structure, automatic data transformation through the Data Reconfiguration Service, keeping duplicate copies consistent, and access controls for privacy of data files.

Their recommendation is that the committee coordinate development in these areas, keep data services consistent and test services in a series of experiments as they are implemented.
sections.eli5: Before trusting the new tools, try them out: move files, rename things, and check that private files stay private.
